chapters.title: Chapter 4: Estimating How Much Capital a Strategy Can Actually Absorb

lessons.title: Position Sizing Under a Capacity Ceiling

children.text: The last lesson produced a number, roughly Rs 17.4 crore of theoretical capacity for the Nifty 50 mean-reversion strategy. A number on its own does not run a book. This closing lesson of the chapter covers how to turn that ceiling into actual day-to-day position sizing rules.
Two Independent Caps on Every Position

markDefs.definition: A risk-management limit on how large any single position can be as a percentage of total portfolio AUM, independent of that stock's liquidity, meant to prevent overconcentration in any one name.

children.text: Every position in the book is actually governed by two separate ceilings. One is the liquidity-derived cap from this chapter, around Rs 1.16 crore per stock in the Nifty 50 example. The other is a

, a plain risk-management rule, say no more than 8 percent of total AUM in any one name, that has nothing to do with liquidity at all. The position size you actually use is whichever of the two is smaller, the binding constraint.

body.caption: Which constraint binds as AUM grows, at an 8% concentration cap and a fixed Rs 1.16 Cr liquidity cap per stock

body.title: Concentration Cap vs Liquidity Cap as AUM Grows

children.text: At small AUM, the concentration cap is the tighter constraint, diversification discipline is doing the work. Past roughly Rs 14.5 crore, the crossover point, the liquidity cap takes over and stays fixed regardless of how much bigger AUM gets. Which rule is actually protecting you changes as the fund grows, even though both rules stay active the entire time.
Why Leave Headroom Below the Theoretical Ceiling

cells: A historical average ADV can look fine on paper while actual daily liquidity is thinner on any given day
The calibration constant Y and the assumption that positions are independent are both simplifications, not guarantees
Chapter 3 showed effective capacity can fall even when your own AUM does not change at all
A crowded unwind, like the August 2007 example, can dry up liquidity exactly when you most need it

body.text: Running a strategy right up to its theoretical capacity leaves no room for any of these four risks to show up at the same time as a bad week. A margin of safety is not conservatism for its own sake, it is what keeps a capacity estimate from becoming a capacity surprise.

body.label: Practical Operating Capacity
body.context: Applying a 65% safety margin to the theoretical Rs 17.4 Cr capacity from the previous lesson: 0.65 x Rs 17.4 Cr

children.text: What Happens as AUM Approaches the Ceiling

As AUM climbs toward the operating capacity, there are a few real options, not just one. Extend the average holding period, which the previous lesson showed is often the single most powerful lever available. Reduce the number of concurrent positions, concentrating capital in the names with the deepest liquidity. Stop raising fresh capital, the soft-close decision covered in Chapter 1 for SEBI-registered AIFs. Or look outside this one strategy entirely, toward a second, complementary strategy that can absorb capital this one cannot, the subject of the next chapter.

body.title: Find the Crossover Point
body.prompt: If the concentration cap were set to 10% of AUM instead of 8%, holding the liquidity cap fixed at Rs 1.16 Cr per stock, at what AUM, in Rs Cr, would the concentration cap and the liquidity cap cross over?
body.explanation: The crossover happens where concentration cap equals liquidity cap: 0.10 x AUM = Rs 1.16 Cr, so AUM = Rs 1.16 Cr / 0.10 = Rs 11.6 Cr. A looser concentration cap moves the crossover point closer in, since concentration stops being the binding constraint sooner.

body.text: A capacity estimate is not a single number you size against. It is two competing constraints, concentration and liquidity, whichever binds tighter at your current AUM, held well inside a safety margin that leaves room for the risks a point estimate cannot see.

points: Every position is governed by two independent ceilings, a liquidity-derived cap and a concentration cap, and the smaller of the two is what actually binds.
Which constraint binds can flip as AUM grows: concentration typically binds at small AUM, liquidity typically binds as AUM approaches the theoretical ceiling.
A practical operating capacity should sit meaningfully below the theoretical ceiling, to leave room for ADV fluctuation, model uncertainty, decay, crowding, and tail liquidity events.

As AUM approaches its operating capacity, the real options are extending holding period, trimming position count, closing to new capital, or diversifying into a complementary strategy, the subject of the next chapter.
